```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

```{r library}
library(diplomacyR)
```

Diplomacy players write orders in a compact shorthand that has been stable
for decades but was never standardised. `dp_parse_orders()` accepts the
spellings people actually use, and `format()` renders any `dp_orders` tibble
back into one canonical form. This vignette is the reference for both.

Every example below is parsed and then rendered back, so the second column is
what the engine understood.

```{r roundtrip-helper}
notation <- function(x, ...) {
  knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Written = x,
    Understood = format(dp_parse_orders(x, ...))
  ))
}
```

## The shape of an order

An order is

```
Power: <unit> <verb> <arguments>
```

The power prefix may be dropped if the `power` argument supplies it instead.
Everything is case-insensitive, and powers may be abbreviated to any
unambiguous prefix.

```{r powers}
notation(c(
  "France: A Par - Bur",
  "FRANCE: A Par - Bur",
  "Fra: A Par - Bur",
  "F: A Par - Bur"
))
```

```{r power-arg}
dp_parse_orders(c("A Par - Bur", "A Mar - Spa"), power = "France")
```

## Locations

Provinces are three-letter codes. Full province names are accepted too and
are translated to codes.

```{r locations}
notation(c(
  "France: A Par - Bur",
  "France: A Paris - Burgundy",
  "France: A paris to burgundy"
))
```

Three provinces on the standard board have two coasts that a fleet cannot
sail between: Spain (`nc`, `sc`), Bulgaria (`ec`, `sc`) and St Petersburg
(`nc`, `sc`). Write the coast after a slash, or in brackets.

```{r coasts}
notation(c(
  "Russia: F Stp/sc - Bot",
  "Russia: F Stp (sc) - Bot",
  "Russia: F STP/SC - BOT",
  "Turkey: F Bul/ec - Bla"
))
```

A coast is only required where the choice is genuinely ambiguous. If exactly
one coast of the destination is reachable, the engine fills it in for you
when it adjudicates; if two are, the order is void and the unit holds.

## Units

`A` and `F` mark armies and fleets, and the long forms `army` and `fleet`
work as well. The designator is optional — the engine reads the real unit
type off the board — but including it is the convention, and it makes an
order set readable on its own.

```{r units}
notation(c(
  "France: A Par - Bur",
  "France: army Par - Bur",
  "France: Par - Bur"
))
```

## Holds

A unit with no verb holds. `H`, `hold`, `holds`, `stand` and `stands` all say
the same thing explicitly.

```{r holds}
notation(c(
  "Austria: A Bud H",
  "Austria: A Bud holds",
  "Austria: A Bud stands",
  "Austria: A Bud"
))
```

## Moves

The move arrow may be a hyphen, an arrow, a dash of any Unicode flavour, or
the word `to`. Spaces around it are optional.

```{r moves}
notation(c(
  "France: A Par - Bur",
  "France: A Par-Bur",
  "France: A Par -> Bur",
  "France: A Par to Bur"
))
```

## Supports

A support either backs a unit that is staying where it is, in which case only
the supported unit's province is named, or backs a move, in which case the
whole move is written out. `S`, `sup`, `supp`, `support` and `supports` are
interchangeable, and the supported unit's own designator is optional.

```{r supports}
notation(c(
  "England: F Lon S F Yor",
  "England: F Lon S Yor",
  "England: F Lon S A Wal - Yor",
  "England: F Lon supports A Wal - Yor"
))
```

## Convoys

A convoy order names the army and its full move. `C`, `conv`, `convoy` and
`convoys` are interchangeable.

```{r convoys}
notation(c(
  "England: F Nth C A Lon - Nwy",
  "England: F Nth convoys A Lon - Nwy",
  "England: F Nth C Lon - Nwy"
))
```

The army being convoyed is ordered to move as usual. Where the destination is
not adjacent, the move is a convoy automatically. Where both a land route and
a sea route exist, append `via convoy` — or `by convoy` — to insist on the
sea route.

```{r via-convoy}
notation(c(
  "England: A Lon - Bel via convoy",
  "England: A Lon - Bel by convoy"
))
```

This is the one distinction `format()` preserves in the rendered output, as
`via Convoy`, because it changes the meaning of the order.

## Retreat phases

The `phase` argument tells the parser which kind of turn the orders belong
to. In a retreat phase a bare move arrow means a retreat; `R`, `retreat` and
`retreats` say so explicitly and work in any phase. A dislodged unit that is
not retreating is removed with `D`, `disband` or `remove`.

```{r retreats}
notation(
  c("Austria: A Tri R Alb",
    "Austria: A Tri retreats Alb",
    "Austria: A Tri - Alb",
    "Austria: A Tri D"),
  phase = "retreat"
)
```

## Adjustment phases

Winter orders build and remove units. Builds must name the unit type, since
there is no unit on the board to read it from; removals need not.

```{r builds}
notation(
  c("Germany: Build A Ber",
    "Germany: Build F Kie",
    "Germany: F Kie B",
    "Germany: Remove F Ber",
    "Germany: Disband A Mun",
    "Germany: A Mun",
    "Germany: Waive"),
  phase = "build"
)
```

Note the last two rows. In an adjustment phase a bare `A Mun` is a removal,
not a hold — there is nothing to hold in a winter turn. `Waive` declines a
build that is owed, which matters when a power would rather not put a unit on
the board.

A fleet built on a split-coast province names its coast the same way a move
does.

```{r build-coast}
notation("Russia: Build F Stp/sc", phase = "build")
```

## Writing several orders at once

`dp_parse_orders()` takes a character vector of orders, but it also splits on
newlines and semicolons, so a whole turn can be pasted in as one string.
Anything after a `#` is a comment.

```{r multiline}
dp_parse_orders(
  "A Par - Bur      # open towards Munich
   A Mar S A Par - Bur
   F Bre - Mao",
  power = "France"
)
```

## Round trips

`format()` renders orders in one canonical spelling: power prefix, unit
designator, three-letter codes with the first letter capitalised, and the
single-letter verbs. Parsing the rendered text gives the same orders back.

```{r canonical}
orders <- dp_example_orders("fall_1901")
canonical <- format(orders)
head(canonical, 4)
```

```{r roundtrip}
identical(format(dp_parse_orders(canonical)), canonical)
```

`as.character()` on a `dp_orders` tibble is the same as `format()`, and
`as_tibble()` strips the class to expose the columns the engine actually
works with.

```{r columns}
as_tibble(dp_parse_orders("England: F Nth C A Lon - Nwy"))
```

## When an order cannot be read

A string that is not an order at all is an error, with the offending piece
named. This is deliberate: a typo in an order set should stop the turn rather
than quietly become a hold.

```{r errors, error = TRUE}
dp_parse_orders("France: A Par flies to Bur")
```

```{r errors-2, error = TRUE}
dp_parse_orders("France: A Xyz - Bur")
```

```{r errors-3, error = TRUE}
dp_parse_orders("A Par - Bur")
```

An order that parses but breaks the rules of the board is a different matter.
Those are accepted here and dealt with by the adjudicator, which converts
them to holds and records why — see `vignette("adjudication")`.
